title: Boils and carbuncles: safe skin care and when drainage is needed
intro: A boil is a painful, pus-filled skin infection, often starting around a hair follicle. Several connected boils can form a larger infected area called a carbuncle. Some small boils settle with simple care, but spreading infection, a sensitive location or particular health risks can make medical treatment necessary. Do not squeeze, pierce or cut a boil yourself: this can spread infection and damage the skin.

sections.heading: Check what the lump is and how it is changing
paragraphs: A boil may begin as a tender lump and become warmer, swollen and filled with pus. Redness can be harder to see on darker skin, so assess pain, heat and swelling too. Not every painful lump is a boil: an inflamed cyst, hidradenitis suppurativa and other conditions can look similar. Tell the clinician about onset, growth, previous episodes, other affected areas and any fever. Mention diabetes, medicines that suppress immunity and a previous resistant bacterial infection, because they can change assessment and treatment.

sections.heading: Use gentle measures without trying to force drainage
paragraphs: For a small uncomplicated boil, a comfortably warm clean compress may ease discomfort and encourage natural drainage. Test the temperature to avoid burns, especially for children or reduced skin sensation. If it opens on its own, gently clean the area, cover it with a clean dressing and wash your hands before and afterwards. Ask a pharmacist which pain medicine suits your health and other medicines. Do not use a needle, repeatedly press out pus or apply harsh household chemicals. Avoid shaving or friction over the inflamed area.

sections.heading: Know when assessment should happen sooner
paragraphs: Seek prompt medical advice for a boil on the face, a large or connected cluster, worsening pain, spreading warmth or swelling, fever or feeling unwell. People with diabetes or weakened immunity should seek earlier advice rather than waiting for a large infection. A lump that does not improve or keeps returning also needs assessment. Rapid deterioration, confusion, collapse or serious breathing difficulty requires emergency help. A small visible opening does not show how far infection extends underneath, and draining a little pus does not prove the problem has resolved.

sections.heading: Discuss professional drainage and antibiotic decisions
paragraphs: A clinician may drain a collection using an appropriate procedure and pain relief. Antibiotics may be needed depending on the location, extent, surrounding infection and your health; they are not automatically the only or necessary treatment for every boil. A swab may help with recurrent infections or treatment that is not working. Tell the team about allergies and earlier antibiotics. Follow the prescribed wound and medicine plan, and ask when to return if pain, swelling or discharge continues. Do not borrow antibiotics or perform a drainage technique seen online.

sections.heading: Reduce spread and investigate repeated episodes
paragraphs: Wash hands after touching the area, keep draining wounds covered and avoid sharing towels, razors or clothing that contacts the infection. Launder used items appropriately and follow advice for sport, swimming or work while a wound is draining. Repeated boils can require assessment for bacterial carriage, skin disease or an underlying health problem. Sometimes a clinician recommends a coordinated treatment for the person or household; do not start disinfectant washes or nasal treatments without instructions. Recurrence is not proof of poor cleanliness, and excessively harsh washing can damage the skin barrier.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: a small boil that starts draining
examples.text: A person uses a clean warm compress on a small boil and it opens naturally. They cover it, wash their hands and monitor pain and swelling. They seek advice if the surrounding skin becomes increasingly hot or painful rather than squeezing out the remaining material.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: repeated painful lumps
examples.text: Someone repeatedly develops painful lumps in the armpits. They arrange a review and describe their locations and earlier treatment. The clinician checks whether these are recurrent boils or a different skin condition, rather than simply repeating another unconfirmed antibiotic course.
